chunk_findings.detail:
The landed check tests the *branch ref* (`wt.branch`), while the run's actual source head is `branch_head`, which for a non-borrowed worktree is taken from the worktree itself (`branch_head = W.head_sha(wt.path)`), not from the ref — the `borrowed` split two lines above exists precisely because these two are not the same source for every caller (and `branch_head` is what the code records as evidence for what was merged). So the code can conclude "landed" from a commit that is not the one this run tried to land.

Concrete input: a non-borrowed item worktree whose HEAD (`branch_head = H`) is ahead of its branch ref, with `wt.branch` pointing at O, an ancestor of `main` (e.g. the worktree carries the item's new commits while the local ref still points at the branch point; ddflow's non-borrowed path deliberately reads the head from `wt.path`, not from `W.rev(repo, wt.branch)`). Run `merge`: `_lands_nothing` sees H has commits `main` lacks, so no refusal; `landed_before = O0`; the `git merge` attempt fails (conflict, or the timeout this change is about) without committing H. H is nowhere on base — the merge gate is reported passed for a merge that never landed, and the item's commits are discarded. Using `branch_head` (or requiring `now` to contain `branch_head`) would test the commit the run was actually merging, consistent with the evidence field written two lines above.

The change assumes the `git add` performed inside the lock determines what gets committed, so that the lock only has to span the whole-line check and staging. That is not how `git commit` with explicit paths works. When paths are given, git runs in `--only` mode, which the git-commit documentation defines as "taking the updated working tree contents of the paths specified on the command line, disregarding any contents that have been staged for other paths." So for the named shards git builds a temporary index from HEAD plus the *current on-disk bytes* of those paths; the blob staged by `git add` under the lock is never used. Minimal demonstration:

```
git init; printf 'old\n' > s; git add s; git commit -m init
printf 'line1\n' >> s; git add s      # staged: whole line "line1"
printf 'line2'  >> s                  # worktree: "line1\nline2" (torn, no newline)

chunk_findings.detail: Previously `W.rev(..., "HEAD")` ran inside `log.transaction()`, so no other *event* commit could move `HEAD` between the commit just made and the SHA read back. Now the lock is released before the commit and the rev: with two doors committing concurrently in the same repo (the parallel-agent scenario this change is motivated by), process A can finish its `git commit`, then B can take the lock, stage and commit its shards, and only then A executes `W.rev(repo, "HEAD")`, returning B's SHA as its own `events_committed`. The events are not lost (A's commit exists as B's parent), but the recorded `events_committed` value no longer identifies the commit that committed the paths it staged, which is what the field is consumed for at the merge/complete door.

chunk_findings.detail: The change fixes the starvation/timeout problem but drops the only mutual exclusion that also covered the git index. Previously the append lock was held across check → `add` → `commit`, so no other ddflow process could touch the index in between; now the window between the release and `git commit` is open. Concrete interleaving in one project (the very situation the change exists for — several ddflow doors running concurrently): door A takes the lock, does the whole-line check, stages the shard and releases; door B then takes the lock, stages its own event line and releases; B's `git commit` completes first. A's `git commit` now runs against the shared index and commits B's staged line (content A never checked/staged, attached to A's commit message), and B's subsequent `git commit` finds nothing to commit and exits non-zero ("nothing to commit, working tree clean"), so a door that did everything right reports failure. If the two commits overlap instead, git's own `.git/index.lock` makes one of them die with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists". This is exactly the "staged paths/content are not the ones this command put there" case: the fix traded a lock that was too coarse for no serialization of the commit at all. The two tests added here (`test_the_staging_runs_under_the_log_lock_and_the_commit_does_not`, `test_another_writer_can_take_the_lock_while_the_commit_hooks_run`) only ever run a single writer, so neither can observe this; keeping the timeout fix requires a commit-level serialization separate from the append lock (or `git commit --only <shard>` plus accepting the same race on that one path), not just moving `git commit` out of the append lock.

chunk_findings.detail: `merge_progress_kwargs` returns `{**merge_kwargs(ctx), "on_progress": lambda line: ...}`, and that value is installed as the action's `call_kwargs` inside the `render_envelope` block. Before this change that slot held only plain data (`merge_kwargs` ends in `return {"shell_cwd": None}`), so whatever renders/encodes the envelope — the `render_envelope` dict exists precisely for that, and the same envelope is what the JSON/ACP consumers see and what gets recorded — received JSON-able values. Now the envelope contains a function object: e.g. `ddflow_merge` invoked through the JSON/ACP path (or any code that does `json.dumps(envelope)` over these kwargs) raises `TypeError: Object of type function is not JSON serializable`, and a text render prints `<function <lambda> at 0x...>`. Either way the observable output on stdout/JSON changes, which is exactly what the stated intent ("No output change on stdout/JSON") promises it does not; the lambda belongs only in the invocation path, not in the dispatched/rendered kwargs. The same commit also adds `wants_progress=True` (mirroring `wants_called_from=True`, which is how the runtime is told to inject a keyword into `call`) while `call_kwargs` already supplies `on_progress` — if the runtime injects it as that flag implies, the merge call itself dies with `TypeError: ... got multiple values for keyword argument 'on_progress'`. Either way the progress plumbing is wired twice into the same call and only one of the two paths can be right.

chunk_findings.detail: The test cannot distinguish the fix from the bug it claims to fix. The docstring says the reported symptom was "the command printed nothing until it finished, and an operator's tool timeout killed what looked like a hang" — i.e. the messages arrived only at the very end, after the post-merge check. This test drives `merge` through `run_cli`, which captures the streams and returns them only when the process exits, then asserts `"merged T1 into main" in err` and `"post-merge check" in err and "[ci].on_merge" in err`. A hypothetical implementation that buffers all three progress lines and flushes them right before `sys.exit`, i.e. exactly the "looks like a hang" behaviour the change exists to remove, passes every assertion here verbatim. Nothing in the test observes the lines while the post-merge check is still running (no `Popen`, no incremental read, no ordering assertion relative to any "check finished"/"done" line), so the property the change promises — visibility *during* a multi-minute wait — is untested. Concretely: replace the progress-emitting code in the merge path with a single `sys.stderr.write(...)` of the same strings placed after the post-merge step, and the suite stays green. The third promised element ("when it finished", per the stated intent) is likewise never asserted at all.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent is that the progress lines go to stderr and that there is "No output change on stdout/JSON", but the test never inspects `out`. It runs `merge` without `--json` and only checks `err`, so an implementation that mistakenly writes these lines to stdout (or that starts emitting them under `--json` and corrupts machine-readable consumers) is not caught. Given input `repo, "merge", "T1", agent="alpha"`, `out` is captured into a local and discarded after the `code == OK` assertion at line 35; adding e.g. `assert out == ""` (and a `--json` variant asserting the JSON still parses) is what would make the "no stdout change" promise verifiable.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new timeout/unavailable branch yields exactly the same value shape as the conflict branch immediately below it (`yield None, ...`). The only difference between the two outcomes is the free-text reason ("could not merge …" vs “… does not merge …”); the first element handed to the caller is `None` in both cases. But the bug being fixed tells us what `yield None` means to this caller: pre-fix, a merge that timed out (killed post-merge hook) took the `if not m.ok` path and produced `yield None, f"{ref} does not merge with {base}: …"`, and the gate recorded **FAILED** 'does not merge'. So `(None, reason)` is the FAILED signal, and the new branch emits the identical signal. Concretely: with a merge that returns `timed_out=True`/`unavailable=True`, control reaches line 128, yields `(None, "could not merge master into work: git merge timed out after 300s")`, returns; a consumer that derives the status from the yielded tuple (as it evidently does for the conflict case) will still classify this as FAILED, not UNAVAILABLE, and the added assertion `res.status == "unavailable" and res.exit == 2` in tests/test_ci_scratch_merge_hooks.py:78 cannot hold.

The only way the added test can pass is if the unchanged caller now switches on the *reason text* rather than on the yielded value. Nothing in this diff introduces or documents such a classifier; in that case the gate's status is coupled to the wording of a user-facing message, so any reword/translation of "could not merge" silently flips UNAVAILABLE back to FAILED (and conversely, the `None` first element still advertises FAILED). Either way the change does not deliver the stated contract: the unavailable outcome needs to be carried by the value the gate classifies (a distinct status/sentinel in the first tuple slot, as the conflict path's `None` carries FAILED), not by the tail of the message.

chunk_findings.detail: The unavailable outcome is gated on `not rep.stale`, so as soon as any pin in the same report is stale, the timeout branch is skipped entirely. In `pins regenerate` (the `check=False` path, i.e. the post-merge hook) the following `if check and rep.stale` guard is also false, so control falls through to the normal "regenerated/ok" return. Concrete input: a tree where pin A is stale (or could not be re-recorded, so its recorded hash still mismatches) and pin B's recipe exceeds `[pins].after_merge_timeout_s` and is appended to `rep.unavailable`. Because `rep.stale` is truthy, the `O.nothing("could not finish: ...")` return is never reached; `check` is false, so the failed branch is never reached either; the call returns the success/current result. Pin B — which the change's stated intent says must be reported UNAVAILABLE, and never stale or failed — is thus folded into an ok outcome, and the only trace is the per-row `unavailable` key that the top-level status no longer reflects. The guard should key off `rep.unavailable` (with stale/failed handled as the higher-severity statuses they are) rather than `rep.unavailable and not rep.stale`, otherwise a pin that could not be checked is silently reported as current whenever it coincides with any stale pin.

chunk_findings.detail: This branch is inconsistent with every other place the code produces an "unavailable" state, and in the normal regenerate flow it leaves the pin flagged stale. The pipeline is check → (not ok) → regenerate → re-check: for the regeneration step to be reached, the check must already have set `st.stale = not ok = True` (`st.stale, st.output = not ok, ...`). The check-timeout branch explicitly undoes that (`st.stale, st.output = False, ""`, with the comment "neither current nor stale"), the lock-contention path builds `PinState(r.name, r.files, unavailable=why)` with `stale` left unset, and the timed-out re-check restores `st.stale` to `was`. The regeneration-timeout branch only assigns `states[r.name].unavailable` and never touches `st.stale`, so a pin that was already stale and whose `r.regen` command runs longer than `limit` ends the run as `stale=True` *and* `unavailable=<timed out>`. Any consumer that reads the per-pin `stale` flag (status summary, stale count, or a renderer that checks `stale` before `unavailable`) will report the timeout as stale content rather than the UNAVAILABLE the change is specified to produce ("report a timeout as UNAVAILABLE (not stale, not failed)"). Concrete input: a pin whose check fails and whose regenerate command exceeds `after_merge_timeout_s` — e.g. check exits 1 (st.stale=True), then `_run(repo, r.regen, r, limit, write=True, tick=tick)` sets `done.timed_out`.

chunk_findings.detail: `st.unavailable` is only ever assigned, never reset (the check-timeout branch sets it and returns `False`; the normal result path sets `st.stale`/`st.output`/`st.seconds` but not `unavailable`). The new `elif st.unavailable:` branch cannot distinguish "this re-check timed out" from "some earlier command in this pin's pipeline timed out", because it keys off that sticky flag. Concrete input: pin P's initial check exceeds `limit` → `st.unavailable = "the check did not finish in Ns (timed out)"`, `st.stale = False`, `ok=False`, so the pipeline proceeds to regenerate P; the regeneration succeeds and a re-check is run; the re-check runs to completion and fails (the pin really is still stale). `check_cmd` sets `st.stale = True` but leaves the stale `st.unavailable` in place, so control takes `elif st.unavailable:` instead of the `else` branch, the "still stale after regeneration" error is dropped, and the comment's claim "nothing is known to be wrong" is recorded although the command did finish and did report a problem — with the timeout message from the *check* now wrongly describing the re-check. Gating on a flag that is not cleared between the check, regeneration and re-check steps means any earlier timeout is mislabelled as the reason for the current state.

chunk_findings.detail: The new unavailability reporting is only consulted on the *later* return paths; the unchanged early exit still returns `""` whenever `rep.problem` is set or `rep.pins` is empty, discarding `cannot` entirely. Concretely: a merge whose regeneration wins nothing — e.g. the per-git-dir lock added by this change is already held by a concurrent `pins regenerate`, or the report is otherwise flagged `problem` — produces a report with no usable pins and/or `problem` set, and the hook prints nothing. Git then shows a clean merge and the user/CI concludes the pins are current, even though no pin was checked; that is exactly the "silently reported current/ok though it could not be checked" outcome the change is meant to prevent (the intended output for that input is the `pins unavailable (not checked, nothing recorded as stale or failed): …` line). Note also that even when it does print, `"; ".join(filter(None, [failed, cannot]))` can emit a line like `pins: a: exit 1; pins unavailable (not checked, nothing recorded as stale or failed): b: timed out`, whose parenthetical claims nothing was recorded as failed while the same line reports a failure — the message contradicts itself whenever `rep.failed` and `rep.unavailable` are both non-empty.

chunk_findings.detail: The change special-cases `m.timed_out or m.unavailable` as UNAVAILABLE, but it keeps `if not m.ok:` immediately below as the *conflict* detector: every other non-zero merge exit is rendered as `f"{ref} {NOT_MERGEABLE} {base}: ..."`, and `run` then reads `NOT_MERGEABLE in failure` and records the gate as `"failed"`. That is the exact defect class the item set out to fix ("a tool that could not finish"), just for failure modes that are not timeouts. Concrete input: the scratch tree is created from `ref` while `base` cannot be resolved there (e.g. `base="main"` and no local `main` in the scratch worktree, or a fetch that lost the remote ref). `merge-base --is-ancestor` returns non-zero for that error too, so the code reaches `W.git(... "merge" ... base)`; git exits 128 with `fatal: 'main' - not something we can merge` (likewise `fatal: Unable to create '.git/index.lock'` under concurrent git activity, or `refusing to merge unrelated histories`). `m.timed_out`/`m.unavailable` are false, so line 133 yields `<ref> does not merge with main: fatal: 'main' - not something we can merge`, line 207 matches `NOT_MERGEABLE`, and the gate is recorded FAILED with a reason asserting a conflict that does not exist — instead of UNAVAILABLE. Detecting "conflict" by `not m.ok` would need at least the merge's own conflict signal (e.g. `CONFLICT (`/`Automatic merge failed` in the output) rather than the mere fact that git exited non-zero.

The change assumes the `git add` performed inside the lock determines what gets committed, so that the lock only has to span the whole-line check and staging. That is not how `git commit` with explicit paths works. When paths are given, git runs in `--only` mode, which the git-commit documentation defines as "taking the updated working tree contents of the paths specified on the command line, disregarding any contents that have been staged for other paths." So for the named shards git builds a temporary index from HEAD plus the *current on-disk bytes* of those paths; the blob staged by `git add` under the lock is never used. Minimal demonstration:

```
git init; printf 'old\n' > s; git add s; git commit -m init
printf 'line1\n' >> s; git add s      # staged: whole line "line1"
printf 'line2'  >> s                  # worktree: "line1\nline2" (torn, no newline)
git commit -q -m x -- s               # commits "line1\nline2", not the staged line1

chunk_findings.detail: The change fixes the starvation/timeout problem but drops the only mutual exclusion that also covered the git index. Previously the append lock was held across check → `add` → `commit`, so no other ddflow process could touch the index in between; now the window between the release and `git commit` is open. Concrete interleaving in one project (the very situation the change exists for — several ddflow doors running concurrently): door A takes the lock, does the whole-line check, stages the shard and releases; door B then takes the lock, stages its own event line and releases; B's `git commit` completes first. A's `git commit` now runs against the shared index and commits B's staged line (content A never checked/staged, attached to A's commit message), and B's subsequent `git commit` finds nothing to commit and exits non-zero ("nothing to commit, working tree clean"), so a door that did everything right reports failure. If the two commits overlap instead, git's own `.git/index.lock` makes one of them die with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists". This is exactly the "staged paths/content are not the ones this command put there" case: the fix traded a lock that was too coarse for no serialization of the commit at all. chunk_findings.detail:
The helper is written as if a failure to resolve the CI command can never harm a merge that has already landed:

```python
try:
    command, why = CI.main_command(repo, cfg)
except Exception:  # a line of progress never stops a merge that has landed
    command, why = "?", ""
if not command:
    return f"post-merge check: nothing to run (...)"
return (
    f"post-merge check starting: [ci].on_merge={cfg.ci.on_merge}, at most "
    f"{cfg.ci.timeout_s}s ([ci].timeout_s); ..."
)
```

Two things go wrong on that path. First, the sentinel `command = "?"` is truthy, so the `if not command` safe return is *skipped* on the exception path — the "nothing to run" branch is unreachable when `main_command` throws. Second, and worse, the function then evaluates `cfg.ci.on_merge` and `cfg.ci.timeout_s` **outside** the `try`, so it dereferences exactly the config object that `CI.main_command` just failed on. Concrete input: a `cfg` whose `[ci]` section has a command/timeout but no `on_merge` key (the change itself says `on_merge` is the *new* key, and configs can pre-date the default being materialised), or any caller that raises while resolving the command. `main_command` returns/raises, the `except` fires, `"?"` is truthy, and `cfg.ci.on_merge` then raises `AttributeError` inside `merge_item` *after* the merge commit has landed. The process dies with a traceback instead of printing a progress line — the same class of failure ("merge landed, the command misbehaved/hung") that this change exists to eliminate, and it directly contradicts the comment's stated guarantee. The `on_progress` callback is only invoked with the final "committing the event log" text afterwards, so nothing is ever delivered for this step. A robust fallback would return a fixed line from the `except` (or move the `cfg.ci.*` formatting inside the guarded block).

chunk_findings.detail: The new accessor is `[p for p in self.pins if p.unavailable and not p.error]`, while `Report.failed` is `[p for p in self.pins if p.error]`. That predicate makes `error` win over `unavailable`, so a pin that the after-merge run recorded as unavailable is *only* classified unavailable if the same pin has no error string. But the after-merge timeout is enforced by the very same `CommandRunner`/`TIMEOUT` path that the pre-existing `[pins].timeout_s` knob documents as "stopped and reported as failed" — i.e. the shared timeout path populates `error`. Concrete input: a recipe whose `check` command hangs under the hook. The runner records the kill in `error`, the after-merge wrapper additionally marks the pin `unavailable`, and the `not p.error` clause then drops it from `unavailable` and hands it to `failed`. The hook therefore reports a timed-out recipe as failed/stale instead of UNAVAILABLE, directly contradicting the contract the new knob states ("reported as UNAVAILABLE (never as failed)"). The same inversion applies to the tree-lock case: any implementation that stores the "another run holds the tree" (or a `LockTimeout` from elsewhere) reason in `error` gets it reclassified as a hard failure rather than the intended unavailable. If the two states must be mutually exclusive, the exclusivity has to be established by construction (set `error = ""` when marking unavailable, or exclude unavailable pins from `failed`), not by a predicate that silently prefers `error`.

`states[r].unavailable` is written by three different phases (the check-timeout branch at ~line 314, the regeneration-timeout branch at ~line 344, and the lock-timeout handler), and nothing added by this change ever clears it; `PinState` is mutated in place and reused for the whole run. The new branch nevertheless assumes the flag means "the re-check did not finish", as its own comment says. That is only true for one of its sources.

Concrete input: a recipe whose *first* check exceeds `limit`. `check_one` sets `st.unavailable = "the check did not finish in ..."`, sets `st.stale = False`, and returns `False` (the value the regeneration flow uses to select the recipe for re-recording). The regeneration command then succeeds, and the re-check runs to completion and returns `False` — i.e. it genuinely reports the pin as still stale. At line 329 `st.unavailable` is still the left-over message from the first phase, so the branch fires, does `st.stale, st.output = was` (the pre-run "current" state) and the `else` that would record `st.error = "still stale after regeneration: ..."` is skipped. The pin ends the run with `stale == False` and no error — reported as not-stale/fine — while the check that just executed said it is stale, and the only surviving text is a stale "the check did not finish (timed out)" message from an earlier phase that no longer describes what happened. The same misclassification occurs for a recipe whose regeneration timed out: the re-check then completes and finds it stale, but the completed verdict is discarded.

Fix: clear `unavailable` before the re-check (or capture the re-check's own outcome) so line 329 only fires when *that* command timed out.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change assumes the `git add` performed inside the lock determines what gets committed, so that the lock only has to span the whole-line check and staging. That is not how `git commit` with explicit paths works. When paths are given, git runs in `--only` mode, which the git-commit documentation defines as "taking the updated working tree contents of the paths specified on the command line, disregarding any contents that have been staged for other paths." So for the named shards git builds a temporary index from HEAD plus the *current on-disk bytes* of those paths; the blob staged by `git add` under the lock is never used. Minimal demonstration:

```
git init; printf 'old\n' > s; git add s; git commit -m init
printf 'line1\n' >> s; git add s      # staged: whole line "line1"
printf 'line2'  >> s                  # worktree: "line1\nline2" (torn, no newline)
git commit -q -m x -- s               # commits "line1\nline2", not the staged line1
```

Applied to ddflow: after `_stage` returns, the append lock is released and `commit_shards` forks `git commit`; git's `prepare_index`/`add_files_to_cache` then re-reads the shard files from disk. Any concurrent ddflow writer that acquires `log.transaction()` in that window (the very contention this change is designed to allow — parallel ddflow commands on one repo) and appends to a shard will have its bytes read by git. chunk_findings.detail: Previously `W.rev(..., "HEAD")` ran inside `log.transaction()`, so no other *event* commit could move `HEAD` between the commit just made and the SHA read back. Now the lock is released before the commit and the rev: with two doors committing concurrently in the same repo (the parallel-agent scenario this change is motivated by), process A can finish its `git commit`, then B can take the lock, stage and commit its shards, and only then A executes `W.rev(repo, "HEAD")`, returning B's SHA as its own `events_committed`. The events are not lost (A's commit exists as B's parent), but the recorded `events_committed` value no longer identifies the commit that committed the paths it staged, which is what the field is consumed for at the merge/complete door.

chunk_findings.detail: The change fixes the starvation/timeout problem but drops the only mutual exclusion that also covered the git index. Previously the append lock was held across check → `add` → `commit`, so no other ddflow process could touch the index in between; now the window between the release and `git commit` is open. Concrete interleaving in one project (the very situation the change exists for — several ddflow doors running concurrently): door A takes the lock, does the whole-line check, stages the shard and releases; door B then takes the lock, stages its own event line and releases; B's `git commit` completes first. A's `git commit` now runs against the shared index and commits B's staged line (content A never checked/staged, attached to A's commit message), and B's subsequent `git commit` finds nothing to commit and exits non-zero ("nothing to commit, working tree clean"), so a door that did everything right reports failure. If the two commits overlap instead, git's own `.git/index.lock` makes one of them die with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists". This is exactly the "staged paths/content are not the ones this command put there" case: the fix traded a lock that was too coarse for no serialization of the commit at all. The two tests added here (`test_the_staging_runs_under_the_log_lock_and_the_commit_does_not`, `test_another_writer_can_take_the_lock_while_the_commit_hooks_run`) only ever run a single writer, so neither can observe this; keeping the timeout fix requires a commit-level serialization separate from the append lock (or `git commit --only <shard>` plus accepting the same race on that one path), not just moving `git commit` out of the append lock.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `gate` lock is held across the entire `git commit` subprocess, and `git commit` runs the project's pre-commit / commit-msg / post-commit hooks. The function's own docstring states the motivating fact — "The hooks of a project can run for minutes (a pre-commit suite)" — and says those hooks must not run inside the append lock. They now run inside `gate` instead, and `gate` is a *global, per-repo* lock that every other `commit_shards` call must take (`with gate:` is the first thing the function does). So the fleet-wide starvation the change set out to remove is still there, just relocated from `.ddflow/events.lock` to `.git/ddflow-eventcommit.lock`, and with the same misleading message the bug report complains about.

Concrete input: a repo whose hook runs the same CI that caused `merge-holds-event-lock-during-ci` (e.g. a pre-commit hook sleeping 120 s), with COMMIT_WAIT_S at its usual 30 s. Door A runs any ddflow command; `commit_shards` takes `gate`, `_stage` returns, and A blocks in `W.git(..., "commit", ...)` while the hook runs. Door B (another agent) runs any ddflow command, calls `commit_shards`, and blocks in `with gate:` for 30 s, then `LockTimeout` is caught and B returns `("", "event log not committed: another event-log commit ran for over 30s")`. Every other agent's command fails the same way for the whole hook duration — exactly the symptom of the bug being fixed, since in practice every ddflow command appends and commits an event. The timeout message is also wrong: nothing is "running a commit" at that point in the sense implied; a user hook is sleeping.

Note this is not the already-confirmed index-window finding: the index is correctly covered now. The defect is that the lock that protects the index is scoped over an arbitrary, operator-supplied subprocess, so its hold time is unbounded and uncommunicated. chunk_findings.detail: The only success criterion of this test is the absence of two substrings in `events_note` (`"nothing to commit"`, `"index.lock"`); it never asserts that either door actually committed anything. Input that makes it green while the change is broken: the second door blocks on the new per-commit lock (the "lock of their own" the docstring relies on) and gives up with the exact failure this bug is about — `events_note: "event log not committed: could not acquire /…/.ddflow/events.lock within 30s"` — or fails with e.g. `fatal: cannot lock ref 'HEAD'`. Neither note contains the two checked substrings, so the loop passes; and because in that design the commit lock is taken *before* the append, the doomed door never appends or stages, so `EC.uncommitted_shards(repo) == []` also holds and the test is fully green even though door `s2`'s session-end event was never written. The test should assert `out.data.get("events_committed")` is present for both doors (and/or that the committed log actually contains both events). This also means the test is not evidence for the confirmed `--only` finding it is cited as probing: on the pre-fix code the append lock was held from the whole-line check through `git commit`, so the two doors were already serialised and the old code likewise produced no `"nothing to commit"`/`"index.lock"` note — the test passes on the unfixed code too, and only reports an *incorrect implementation* of the fix.

chunk_findings.detail: The interleaving the test exists to exercise is created by a fixed sleep, not by synchronisation with the first door's state. If the first thread has not reached its commit within 0.4 s (loaded CI, slow first `git add`, lock acquisition), the second door runs entirely after the first has finished, the race never happens, and the test passes without testing anything — a silent false negative for exactly the concurrent-commit scenario it was added to guard. A deterministic handshake (e.g. have the pre-commit hook signal when it has entered the commit, and start the second door from there) is needed for the assertion to mean anything.

chunk_findings.detail: `_ci_notice` is documented as "a line of progress never stops a merge that has landed", and `say(_ci_notice(repo, cfg))` runs after `W.merge` has landed but before `check_after_merge` and `EC.commit_at(log, cfg, "merge", ...)`. The only guarded expression is `CI.main_command(repo, cfg)`. Its handler then sets `command, why = "?", ""`, and because `"?"` is truthy the `if not command:` early-return (the only path that avoids touching the config's CI knobs) is skipped, so the final f-string evaluates `cfg.ci.on_merge` and `cfg.ci.timeout_s` unguarded. The very situation the `try` exists for — `CI.main_command` raising while reading the `[ci]` section (e.g. a config whose `ci` section lacks the new `on_merge`, or an older/partial config where `cfg.ci` is `None`) — therefore re-raises `AttributeError` from the `cfg.ci.on_merge` lookup, after the commit has already landed. The merge then aborts before `check_after_merge` and `EC.commit_at`, so the event log is never committed and the command exits non-zero on an already-landed merge, which is exactly the "landed but the command failed afterwards" class this item is about. Guarding the fallback (or returning the "nothing to run" string whenever `main_command` raises) would be safe.

chunk_findings.detail: This finding (#1 from the earlier review) still holds, and the named probe does not answer it. The production change visible here is only the new function, and its body is unchanged from the description of the bug: it returns `{**merge_kwargs(ctx), "on_progress": lambda line: print(...)}`, i.e. a dict whose value is a live callable. Per the context, that return value is installed as the action's `call_kwargs` inside the `render_envelope(...)` block, so the envelope that JSON/ACP consumers read and that gets recorded still carries a non-JSON-serializable object. The probe that triage attached to this item is `tests/test_merge_progress.py::test_json_output_is_unchanged_and_progress_stays_on_stderr_and_live`, which drives the CLI (`--json`) and asserts the *stdout* text is byte-identical. That only exercises one consumer on one path: it cannot show that the ACP consumer or the recorded/ledgered envelope (the other two destinations the finding named) can encode a callable, and a passing test does not remove the callable from `call_kwargs`. So the demonstrated failure mode remains: anything that serializes the `render_envelope` payload — `json.dumps(envelope)` on the ACP path, or persisting the recorded envelope — raises `TypeError: Object of type function is not JSON serializable` (or, with a custom default, silently embeds a placeholder). To answer it, the callable must be kept out of the envelope data (e.g. pass `on_progress` through a side channel, or have `render_envelope` extract/strip callables from `call_kwargs` before building the serializable payload); the new CLI test alone is not a fix.

chunk_findings.detail:
The helper is written as if a failure to resolve the CI command can never harm a merge that has already landed:

```python
try:
    command, why = CI.main_command(repo, cfg)
except Exception:  # a line of progress never stops a merge that has landed
    command, why = "?", ""
if not command:
    return f"post-merge check: nothing to run (...)"
return (
    f"post-merge check starting: [ci].on_merge={cfg.ci.on_merge}, at most "
    f"{cfg.ci.timeout_s}s ([ci].timeout_s); ..."
)
```

Two things go wrong on that path. First, the sentinel `command = "?"` is truthy, so the `if not command` safe return is *skipped* on the exception path — the "nothing to run" branch is unreachable when `main_command` throws. Second, and worse, the function then evaluates `cfg.ci.on_merge` and `cfg.ci.timeout_s` **outside** the `try`, so it dereferences exactly the config object that `CI.main_command` just failed on. Concrete input: a `cfg` whose `[ci]` section has a command/timeout but no `on_merge` key (the change itself says `on_merge` is the *new* key, and configs can pre-date the default being materialised), or any caller that raises while resolving the command. `main_command` returns/raises, the `except` fires, `"?"` is truthy, and `cfg.ci.on_merge` then raises `AttributeError` inside `merge_item` *after* the merge commit has landed. The process dies with a traceback instead of printing a progress line — the same class of failure ("merge landed, the command misbehaved/hung") that this change exists to eliminate, and it directly contradicts the comment's stated guarantee. The `on_progress` callback is only invoked with the final "committing the event log" text afterwards, so nothing is ever delivered for this step. A robust fallback would return a fixed line from the `except` (or move the `cfg.ci.*` formatting inside the guarded block).

chunk_findings.detail: The 60 s `deadline` is only evaluated *between* calls to `p.stderr.readline()`, and `readline()` blocks indefinitely as long as the child still holds the write end of the stderr pipe. So if the merge hangs after landing without emitting `post-merge check starting` — precisely the failure mode this file exists to guard ("the command then kept running past a 120 s tool timeout, printing nothing until it finished") — the loop blocks inside `readline()` forever and the test never reaches the `assert ... , seen` at line 84 nor the `finally`'s `p.communicate(timeout=120)`. The test suite then hangs until whatever outer timeout the harness imposes instead of failing fast; give the subprocess a hard deadline (e.g. `p.wait(timeout=...)`/a watchdog thread) rather than relying on the in-loop clock check. (Secondary, same loop: once the child exits without ever printing the line, `readline()` returns `""` immediately, so the loop degenerates into a 60 s busy spin appending the empty string.)

chunk_findings.detail: The new timeout branch flags `states[r.name].unavailable` but—unlike the sibling check-timeout branch two hunks above, which explicitly does `st.stale, st.output = False, ""` to record "neither current nor stale"—it never clears `st.stale`, and it does not clear `st.output` either. The only new compensation in this diff is the `elif st.unavailable:` arm of the re-check, but that arm just executes `st.stale, st.output = was`, i.e. it restores the state captured when the re-check started. For a pin whose re-record just timed out, that state is still the initial check's verdict `(True, <tail of the failed check>)`: the reset back to `(False, "")` only lives in the re-record *success* branch (the `else:` after this hunk), which a timed-out run never reaches, and the driver cannot have reset it either—otherwise the confirmed finding ("in the normal regenerate flow it leaves the pin flagged stale") would not have reproduced in the first place. So the concrete outcome is unchanged from the reported bug: pin P fails its check, its re-record exceeds `limit` under load, and P still ends the run in the stale set (with a stale `output`), so the report/`pin_files.py` distinction `rep.unavailable and not rep.stale` keys off `stale=True` and P is presented as stale rather than as "the command did not finish; its files may be half written". The probe `tests/test_pins_after_merge_safe.py::test_a_regeneration_that_times_out_is_not_reported_as_current` only asserts the pin is not reported *current*, which is equally true of a pin that is reported stale, so it does not exercise this path; the `elif st.unavailable:` arm also cannot fix it, since in this path `was` already carries `stale=True`.

chunk_findings.detail: The change converts an interrupted regeneration into a *report-only* outcome: when the regen command is killed at the (now shorter) `limit`, the branch only sets `states[r.name].unavailable = "...its files may be half written, check \`git status\`..."` and prints a line; it does not revert, retry, or otherwise restore the pin files, and `st.stale` is left as it was. chunk_findings.detail:
The new UNAVAILABLE text is assembled *after* the early return:

```python
rep = regenerate(repo, cfg, after_merge=True, on_progress=_say)
if rep.problem or not rep.pins:
    return ""                      # <-- cannot is not built yet
cannot = ( ... rep.unavailable ... )
```

so whenever `regenerate` records a run-level `problem`, `after_merge` returns the empty string and the unavailability of the pins that timed out (or were otherwise not checked) is never printed — the exact behaviour the help text added in this diff promises ("reported as UNAVAILABLE (never as failed) and the hook exits cleanly").

The triage marks this refuted with `tests/test_pins_after_merge_safe.py::test_the_hook_says_so_when_another_run_holds_the_tree`, but that probe only exercises the lock-held path, which is precisely the branch that *does* reach `cannot`: there `rep.problem` is falsy and `rep.pins` is non-empty (the pins are in `rep.pins` as unavailable entries, so the guard passes). The probe never sets `rep.problem`, so it cannot and does not answer the claim for the branch that drops the message. Concrete input: a merge under load where one recipe exceeds `after_merge_timeout_s` (its pin goes into `rep.unavailable`) and regenerate additionally records a run-level problem (e.g. a pin write/README-growth refusal). `rep.problem` is truthy, `after_merge` returns `""` at that line, git prints nothing about the timed-out recipe, and the user is left believing every pin was checked. Note the `not rep.pins` half of the guard is harmless for this bug (`Report.unavailable` is a comprehension over `self.pins`, so an empty `rep.pins` implies an empty `cannot`); it is the `rep.problem` half that still drops the line, and moving the `cannot` computation above the guard (and including it in that return) would fix it.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change assumes the `git add` performed inside the lock determines what gets committed, so that the lock only has to span the whole-line check and staging. That is not how `git commit` with explicit paths works. When paths are given, git runs in `--only` mode, which the git-commit documentation defines as "taking the updated working tree contents of the paths specified on the command line, disregarding any contents that have been staged for other paths." So for the named shards git builds a temporary index from HEAD plus the *current on-disk bytes* of those paths; the blob staged by `git add` under the lock is never used. Minimal demonstration:

```
git init; printf 'old\n' > s; git add s; git commit -m init
printf 'line1\n' >> s; git add s      # staged: whole line "line1"
printf 'line2'  >> s                  # worktree: "line1\nline2" (torn, no newline)
git commit -q -m x -- s               # commits "line1\nline2", not the staged line1
```

Applied to ddflow: after `_stage` returns, the append lock is released and `commit_shards` forks `git commit`; git's `prepare_index`/`add_files_to_cache` then re-reads the shard files from disk. Any concurrent ddflow writer that acquires `log.transaction()` in that window (the very contention this change is designed to allow — parallel ddflow commands on one repo) and appends to a shard will have its bytes read by git. chunk_findings.detail: Previously `W.rev(..., "HEAD")` ran inside `log.transaction()`, so no other *event* commit could move `HEAD` between the commit just made and the SHA read back. Now the lock is released before the commit and the rev: with two doors committing concurrently in the same repo (the parallel-agent scenario this change is motivated by), process A can finish its `git commit`, then B can take the lock, stage and commit its shards, and only then A executes `W.rev(repo, "HEAD")`, returning B's SHA as its own `events_committed`. chunk_findings.detail: The change fixes the starvation/timeout problem but drops the only mutual exclusion that also covered the git index. Previously the append lock was held across check → `add` → `commit`, so no other ddflow process could touch the index in between; now the window between the release and `git commit` is open. Concrete interleaving in one project (the very situation the change exists for — several ddflow doors running concurrently): door A takes the lock, does the whole-line check, stages the shard and releases; door B then takes the lock, stages its own event line and releases; B's `git commit` completes first. A's `git commit` now runs against the shared index and commits B's staged line (content A never checked/staged, attached to A's commit message), and B's subsequent `git commit` finds nothing to commit and exits non-zero ("nothing to commit, working tree clean"), so a door that did everything right reports failure. If the two commits overlap instead, git's own `.git/index.lock` makes one of them die with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists". This is exactly the "staged paths/content are not the ones this command put there" case: the fix traded a lock that was too coarse for no serialization of the commit at all. The two tests added here (`test_the_staging_runs_under_the_log_lock_and_the_commit_does_not`, `test_another_writer_can_take_the_lock_while_the_commit_hooks_run`) only ever run a single writer, so neither can observe this; keeping the timeout fix requires a commit-level serialization separate from the append lock (or `git commit --only <shard>` plus accepting the same race on that one path), not just moving `git commit` out of the append lock.

chunk_findings.detail: The whole-line check and the commit are no longer atomic: `_stage` runs `whole()` + `git add` under `hold()` at :103-104, but `hold` is released before `W.git(repo, "commit", ..., "--", *shards)` at :108, and plain event appenders take only the append lock (`hold`) — never the `gate`, which is acquired only inside `commit_shards`. Since `git commit -- <paths>` is `--only` mode and reads the *working tree* at commit time (as the new docstring itself concedes), a shard that passed `whole()` can be half-written by a concurrent appender when git reads it, and the torn line is committed into history. The new post-hoc `_committed_whole` check at :111-115 does not prevent this: it runs after the commit, only appends a note to `skipped`, and still returns `W.rev(repo, "HEAD")` as success ("committed with a half-written last line"). This is prior finding #1 still holding, and it is a regression against the pre-change behaviour: because check→add→commit used to sit entirely under the append lock, a shard being written was left out of the commit (`left out, being written or unreadable`) — the very `whole()`/`skipped` machinery exists because half-written `jsonl` lines are an observed state, so the docstring's "ddflow appends a line in one write" premise is contradicted by the code it replaced. Interleaving: door A lists shard S as whole and releases the append lock; door B (append-only path, does not take `gate`) is mid-write on S; A's `git commit --only -- S` reads the partial line and commits it; the fragment is now in git history and the remainder of B's line is appended after it, corrupting one event for every consumer that parses the log line by line.

chunk_findings.detail: The planner now builds the entire commit tree by seeding a private index from `HEAD` (`read-tree HEAD`) plus only the shards it read as `taken`, and the real `git commit` runs later, after `hold` has been released. Because the index carries the *whole* HEAD tree, not just the named shards, a commit made from a snapshot that has gone stale rewrites every file in that tree back to its plan-time content. Concrete interleaving with two doors in one repo (the scenario this change exists for): `a.jsonl` = `l1` and `b.jsonl` = `m1` are committed. Door B takes the event lock, computes `taken` (a.jsonl is not listed as uncommitted, so it is absent from B's index beyond its `l1` copy from `read-tree HEAD`) and read-trees HEAD; B then releases the lock but has not yet committed. Door A appends `l2` to a.jsonl (appends need no lock), takes the lock, plans against HEAD (a.jsonl = `l1`), commits — HEAD now has a.jsonl = `l1\nl2`. Door B now runs its commit from the index it built from the old HEAD; that tree still contains a.jsonl = `l1`, so B's commit silently reverts A's line. The previous implementation did `git commit -- <its own shards>`, i.e. `--only` mode, and never rewrote paths it was not asked about, so this reversion is new. The confirmed probe (`test_two_doors_committing_at_once_do_not_commit_each_others_stage`) only exercises index isolation, not this stale-HEAD reversion, so it does not answer it.

For a pin whose re-record just timed out, that state is still the initial check's verdict `(True, <tail of the failed check>)`: the reset back to `(False, "")` only lives in the re-record *success* branch (the `else:` after this hunk), which a timed-out run never reaches, and the driver cannot have reset it either—otherwise the confirmed finding ("in the normal regenerate flow it leaves the pin flagged stale") would not have reproduced in the first place. The change assumes the `git add` performed inside the lock determines what gets committed, so that the lock only has to span the whole-line check and staging. chunk_findings.detail: The change fixes the starvation/timeout problem but drops the only mutual exclusion that also covered the git index. Previously the append lock was held across check → `add` → `commit`, so no other ddflow process could touch the index in between; now the window between the release and `git commit` is open. chunk_findings.detail: `_snapshot` builds the private index "on top of HEAD" while `hold()` is held (call it H1) and the commit is made after `hold()` is released. `git commit` with `GIT_INDEX_FILE` (and no pathspec) creates a commit *whose tree is the index*: H1's tree with the shards replaced. Meanwhile the gate lock only serialises event commits — it does not stop a user's `git commit`, another `ddflow` door's merge/complete commit, etc. Concrete interleaving in the multi-agent repo this change exists for: agent A calls `commit_shards`, snapshots from HEAD=H1, releases the append lock; before A's `git` subprocess resolves HEAD, agent B's merge lands H2 (touching the working tree/other files); A's `git commit` then runs with parent H2 but with H1's tree, so every change H2 introduced is absent from the new HEAD. Because HEAD moves to A's commit, B's work is silently undone at the branch tip (the files are left "modified" in the working tree for whoever looks next). The previous code could not do this: `git commit -- <paths>` is `--only` mode, which rebuilds the tree from the *then current* HEAD with the named paths taken from the working tree, so an intervening commit's other changes were preserved. Fixing it needs the private index to be re-based on HEAD immediately before committing (still inside the gate), or an explicit check that HEAD has not moved since `_snapshot`.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten staging captures the *whole base tree* by snapshotting `HEAD` at staging time (`git read-tree HEAD` into the alternate index), while the actual `git commit` is deliberately moved outside this lock (that is the point of the change, and finding #4 confirms the commit runs later inside a separate `gate`). The commit therefore creates a tree derived from the old `HEAD` snapshot but with the *current* `HEAD` as its parent. Any commit that lands between this `read-tree` and the gated `git commit` and that is not itself serialised by `gate` is silently reverted in history. Concretely: `ddflow complete X` runs `_prepare` at `HEAD=t0`; a concurrent `ddflow merge Y` (the exact fleet scenario in this bug report; its merge commit is created by `git merge`, not by `commit_shards`, and finding #4 notes the gated commit can be held for minutes by pre-commit hooks) lands commit `t1` touching e.g. `ddflow/tasks/...`; when the complete door finally commits the staged index, its tree is `t0`'s tree plus the event shards while its parent is `t1`, so `git diff t1 HEAD` shows all of `t1` undone. The old `git add` + `git commit -- <paths>` (--only) built the base from `HEAD` at commit time and did not have this failure mode; the temp-index design must either be wrapped by the same lock as every other committer in the repo or re-base (`read-tree` current `HEAD`, then re-apply the captured blobs) immediately before committing.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten staging captures the *whole base tree* by snapshotting `HEAD` at staging time (`git read-tree HEAD` into the alternate index), while the actual `git commit` is deliberately moved outside this lock (that is the point of the change, and finding #4 confirms the commit runs later inside a separate `gate`). Any commit that lands between this `read-tree` and the gated `git commit` and that is not itself serialised by `gate` is silently reverted in history. If `gate` were the same file, this probe would have read `"held"` and failed, so the probe passing proves only that the commit no longer holds `events.lock` — it says nothing about `gate`. Since the triage leaves the cited line `with gate:` around the whole `git commit` in place (it is marked `refuted`, not superseded), the pre-commit/commit-msg/post-commit hooks — which the function's own docstring says "can run for minutes (a pre-commit suite)" — still execute while `gate` is held. Concrete input: door A runs `commit_shards` (`ddflow merge`) and its pre-commit suite runs for minutes inside `with gate:`; door B (the `ddflow complete` in the bug report, which also commits when `commit_events_at` is set) reaches its own `commit_shards` and must take the same `gate`, so it blocks for the whole hook — or, if `gate` carries the same 30 s acquisition timeout, dies with the very "could not acquire … lock within 30s … Another agent may be wedged" message the change was meant to remove. The fix has moved the fleet-wide serialisation from `events.lock` to `gate` instead of eliminating it, and no test in this diff exercises that lock.
